Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 41, verses 6–8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ ﴿who do not give zakah﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations:

First: He rebuked them for stinginess (shuhh), which noble people find shameful. In this there is an indication that the disbeliever is punished for his disbelief, together with the obligation of zakah upon him, more than one who is not obligated to pay zakah is punished. This was said by Ibn Isa.

Second: its meaning is that they do not purify their deeds. This was said by Ibn Umar.

Third: its meaning is that they do not bring it (zakah) as pure (azkiya'). This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: its meaning is that they do not believe in zakah. This was said by Qatadah.

Fifth: its meaning is that they are not among the people of zakah. This was said by Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them is a reward that will not be cut off﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations:

First: not counted (ghayr mahsub). This was said by Mujahid.

Second: not diminished (ghayr manqus). This was said by Ibn Abbas and Qutrub, and he recited the verse of Zuhayr:

"The excellence of the swift horses over the slow ones; it does not give, by that, one who is reckoned (mamnun) nor one who is wanton (nazaq)."

Third: not interrupted (ghayr maqtu'). This was said by Ibn Isa, derived from "mananta al-habl" meaning "I cut the rope." Dhu al-Usba' al-Adwani said:

"By your life, my door is not one with a lock against the friend, nor is my goodness one that is cut off (mamnun)."

Fourth: not bestowed upon them with reproach (ghayr mamnun 'alayhim bihi). This was said by al-Suddi.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun*) on Surah 41, verses 9–12:**

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He created it on the two days of Sunday and Monday. Creating it over two days is a stronger proof of power and wisdom than creating it all at once in the blink of an eye, because it is further from being attributed to chance or to mere nature, and so that He might guide His creation to deliberateness (*al-anāh*) in their affairs.

﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: they are likenesses (*ashbāh*). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are partners (*shurakāʾ*). This is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah.

The third: they are equals (*kufuwan*) among men whom you obey in acts of disobedience to God, Exalted is He. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fourth: it is the saying of a man, "If it were not for So-and-so's dog, the thieves would have come," and "If it were not for So-and-so, such-and-such would have happened." This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it﴾. That is, mountains. Regarding their being called *rawāsī* (firm/anchoring), there are two aspects:

One: because the peaks of these mountains are high.

Two: because the earth is anchored by them, or because they are firmly established upon the earth.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾. On this there are two aspects:

One: that is, He made its trees grow without planting and brought forth its crops without seed. This was said by al-Suddi.

Two: He deposited in it the benefits for its people. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾. On this there are four interpretations:

One: He determined the provisions of its inhabitants. This was said by al-Hasan.

Two: He determined in it its interests, from its mountains, seas, rivers, trees and animals. This was said by Qatadah.

Three: He determined in it its sustenance from the rain. This was said by Mujahid.

Four: He determined in each region of it what He did not place in another, so that some of them might sustain others through trade from one land to another. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

﴿In four days﴾: that is, the completion of four days. From this is the saying of one who says: "I went out from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning, in the completion of fifteen days.

It has also come in the raised (*marfūʿ*) hadith: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and created the mountains on Tuesday, and on Wednesday He created the trees, the water, the wasteland and the inhabited land. These are four days. And on Thursday He created the heaven, and on Friday He created the stars, the sun, the moon, the angels and Adam."

Regarding His creating them one thing after another, there are two views:

One: so that the angels who were present might take a lesson from it.

Two: so that the worshippers who were informed might take a lesson from it.

﴿Equally for those who ask﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

One: equally for those who ask about the term of the period in God's creation of the earth. This was said by Qatadah.

Two: equally for those who ask about their sustenance and provisions.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾. On this there are two aspects:

One: He intended the heaven. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

Two: His command turned toward the heaven. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿He said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly﴾. On this there are two views:

One: that He said this before their creation, and the meaning of "come" is "be," so they came into being, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Two: the view of the majority is that He said this to them after creating them.

Accordingly, its meaning has four interpretations:

One: its meaning is, "Give obedience in the course that has been determined for you, willingly or unwillingly," that is, by choice or by compulsion. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Two: "Come to My worship and knowledge, willingly or unwillingly, by choice or not by choice."

Three: "Come with what is in you, willingly or unwillingly." This was related by al-Naqqash.

Four: "Be as I have commanded, in hardness and softness, in sorrow and ease, in what is unyielding and what is pliable." This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Regarding His saying ﴿to it﴾ there are two aspects:

One: that it is a speech He uttered.

Two: that it is a power from Him that became manifest to them, and it took the place of speech in attaining the desired end.

﴿They said: We come willingly﴾. On this there are three sayings:

One: its meaning is, "We have given obedience." This was narrated by Tawus.

Two: "We have come with what is in us."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The heaven came with what is in it of the sun, the moon and the stars, and the earth came with what is in it of trees, rivers and fruits.

Three: its meaning is, "As God willed that we should be." This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Regarding their saying, there are two aspects:

One: that the manifestation of obedience from them stood in the place of their saying.

Two: that they both spoke with that.

Abu al-Nasr al-Sakaski said: The place of the Kaʿba spoke from the earth, and what lies opposite it spoke from the heaven, so God placed His sanctuary in it.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾. That is, He created them as seven heavens in two days. It has been said: Thursday and Friday. Al-Suddi said: It was called Friday (*al-Jumʿa*) because the creation of the heavens and the creation of the earths were gathered (*jumiʿa*) in it.

A group said: He created the heavens before the earths, on Sunday and Monday, and He created the earths and the mountains on Tuesday and Wednesday, and He created what is other than these two of the world on Thursday and Friday. A third group said that He created the heaven as smoke before the earth, then He split it into seven heavens after the earths. God knows best what He did. The views differ on this, and there is no room for *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) in it.

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾. On this there are three aspects:

One: its meaning is that He settled its angels in each heaven. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Two: He created in each heaven its creation. He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars and its good order. This was said by Qatadah.

Three: He revealed to the inhabitants of each heaven among the angels what He commanded them of worship. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a protection﴾. That is, We made it an adornment and a protection.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 41, verses 33–36:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾, and so on.

On this there are two views:

First: that it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

Second: that it refers to the believers who called to Allah. This was said by Qays ibn Abi Hazim and Mujahid.

﴿And does righteous deeds﴾. On this there are two views:

First: that it means performing the obligatory duties (al-fara'id). This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: that it refers to those who pray two rak'ahs between the adhan and the iqamah. This was said by Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Hisham ibn Urwah narrated from Aisha that she said: "When Bilal would stand to call the adhan, the Jews would say, 'A crow has stood up, no, it has not stood up,' and then he called to prayer. And when they bowed in prayer, they would say, 'They have knelt, no, they have not knelt.' So this verse was revealed concerning Bilal and those who pray."

His words, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾. On this there are six interpretations: (p-182)

First: that the good (al-hasanah) is forbearance (al-mudarah), and the evil (al-sayyi'ah) is harshness (al-ghilzah). This was related by Ibn Isa.

Second: the good is patience (al-sabr), and the evil is aversion (al-nufur).

Third: the good is faith (al-iman), and the evil is polytheism (al-shirk). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: the good is pardon (al-'afw), and the evil is retaliation (al-intisar). This was related by Ibn Umayr.

﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: that is, who created these signs.

The second: at His saying ﴿and they are not wearied﴾. Said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: dead and dry, said by al-Suddi.

It may also bear a third meaning: humbled by drought, because it is forsaken; and when it becomes fertile it is honored, because it is inhabited.

﴿So when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.﴾ In it there are two aspects:

The first: it stirs with movement for the plants, and swells with rising before it sprouts, said by Mujahid.

The second: it stirs with vegetation and swells with the abundance of its produce, said by al-Kalbi.

Thus, according to Mujahid's view, there is an inversion in the order, its sense being: it swelled and then stirred.

Regarding His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who distort [or deviate concerning] Our signs﴾, there are five interpretations:

First: they deny Our signs. This is said by Qatadah.

Second: they turn away from Our signs. This is said by Abu Malik.

Third: they disbelieve in Us. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: they oppose Our messengers. This is said by al-Suddi.

Fifth: it refers to whistling (al-muka') and clapping (al-tasfiq) during the recitation of the Qur'an. This is said by Mujahid.

﴿They are not hidden from Us﴾, and this is a warning.

﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ Regarding this, there are four statements: (p-185) 

First: the one thrown into the Fire is Abu Jahl, and the one who comes secure is Ammar ibn Yasir. This is said by Ikrimah.

Second: the one thrown into the Fire is Abu Jahl, and the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection is Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). This is said by Ibn Ziyad.

Third: the one thrown into the Fire is Abu Jahl and his companions. This is said by al-Kalbi. The one who comes secure is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is said by Muqatil.

Fourth: it is general: the one thrown into the Fire is the disbeliever, and the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection is the believer. This is said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿Do whatever you wish﴾, this is a threat.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾, a warning; thus He threatened and warned.

Regarding His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾, the Reminder here is the Qur'an, according to all. It has an omitted response, its implied meaning being: they are destroyed, or they will be punished.

﴿And indeed, it is a Book of might﴾, regarding this there are two aspects:

One: it is mighty against Satan, that he could alter it. This is said by al-Suddi.

Second: it is impossible for people to produce the like of it. This is said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿Falsehood does not approach it﴾. Regarding "falsehood" here there are four statements:

First: it is Iblis. This is said by Qatadah.

Second: it is Satan. This is said by Ibn Jurayj.

Third: it is alteration. This is said by Mujahid.

Fourth: it is punishment. This is said by Sa'id.

And it may allow a fifth: that falsehood is contradiction and discord.

﴿From before it or from behind it﴾. Regarding this there are three aspects:

First: falsehood does not reach it from a Book before it, nor from a Book after it. This is said by Qatadah.

Second: falsehood does not reach it from the beginning of the revelation nor from its end.

(p-186) Third: falsehood does not reach it in its reports of what came before, nor in its reports of what came after. This is said by Ibn Jurayj.

And it may allow a fourth: "what is before it" is its wording, and "what is behind it" is its interpretation; so falsehood does not reach it in wording or in interpretation. ﴿A revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy﴾. Qatadah said: "Wise in His command, Praiseworthy toward His creation."

Regarding His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects:

One: what the polytheists say to you is only what those before them said to their prophets, that he is a sorcerer or a madman. This is said by Qatadah.

Second: you only report what the prophets before you reported, namely ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Forgiving, and Possessor of painful punishment﴾. This was related by Ibn Isa, and said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 41, verse 44–45:

The second: in a non-Arabic tongue.

﴿They would have said: "Why have its verses not been made distinct?"﴾ That is, why have its verses not been explained to us in Arabic according to the second interpretation, while according to the first, the meaning is "why have its verses not been made eloquent (al-fasah)?"

One: how can the Qur'an be non-Arabic when Muhammad (ﷺ) is an Arab? This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: how can the Qur'an be non-Arabic when we are an Arab people? This was said by al-Suddi.

(p-187) ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing.﴾ This may bear two interpretations:

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 41, verses 49–51:

His statement, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾. That is, he does not grow weary of asking for good. Here "good" means wealth and health, as said by al-Suddi. And "man" here refers to the disbeliever.

﴿But if evil touches him, he becomes despairing, utterly hopeless﴾. This means poverty and sickness. It may bear two meanings:

The first: he despairs of good and loses hope in mercy.

The second: he despairs of the answering of supplication, and thinks ill of his Lord.

His statement, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾. It may bear two meanings:

The first: ease after hardship.

The second: wealth after poverty.

﴿He will surely say, "This is mine."﴾ In this there are two meanings:

The first: this is by my own effort.

The second: this is by my own merit.

﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come to pass﴾. This is a denial on his part of resurrection and recompense, despite the blessing and ease he has been granted and the harm and trial he has been spared.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him﴾, and so on.

If it is as you claim, that there is a return and recompense, then I will have with Him in the future the like of what He has given me in the present.

It has also been said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

His statement, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws to his side﴾. It may bear three meanings:

The first: he turns away from faith and keeps far from what is obligatory.

The second: he turns away from gratitude and strays far from right guidance.

The third: he turns away from obedience and keeps far from acceptance.

﴿But when evil touches him, he has long supplication﴾. In this there are two meanings:

The first: complete, because his desire in it is sincere.

(p-189)The second: abundant, because of the continuity of his persistence in it. This is the meaning of al-Suddi's statement. The complete and the abundant are described as "long-stretched" (ʿarīḍ) rather than "long" (ṭawīl), because ʿarḍ combines length and breadth, so it is more comprehensive. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The disbeliever knows his Lord in affliction, and does not know Him in ease.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾. In this there are five opinions:

The third: that they are: on the horizons, the signs of the sky; and within themselves, the events of the earth.

The first: it becomes clear to them that the Qur'an is the truth.

The second: that what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought them and invited them to is the truth.

The first: His knowledge encompasses all things. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The second: His power encompasses all things. This is the saying of al-Kalbi.
